What the research says about learning to code

We have tried to be careful. We cite real studies, we say how strong the evidence is, and we do not promise grades, jobs or college places.

How to read this page

Strong: several careful studies agree. Mixed: results vary or shrink in the strictest studies. Open question: we do not know yet. Click the study names to jump to the full reference at the bottom.

  • Why now
  • What the research shows
  • What good teaching looks like
  • References

Why now

How computing and AI are changing the skills children will need, and how much computer science schools offer.

Computing is changing the skills our kids need

In plain language

This is a survey of what employers expect, not a measurement of the future. Forecasts like this are useful for direction, not for precise predictions.

More detail on this slide

The World Economic Forum surveys large employers worldwide every two years. In the January 2025 report, the three skills expected to grow fastest by 2030 are AI and big data; networks and cybersecurity; and technological literacy. Analytical thinking remains the skill employers most often call essential (seven in ten). Stress the take-away: we are not trying to turn ten-year-olds into software engineers. We want them to understand, question and shape the technology they will grow up with.

A question parents often ask

Will coding guarantee my child a good job?
No, and nobody can promise that. What we can say is that understanding how computers and AI work is becoming a basic literacy, like understanding money or science.

Source: World Economic Forum (2025), a survey of over 1,000 employers.

Schools are still catching up

In plain language

These numbers describe US public high schools. Elementary schools are measured differently, so we do not quote a figure for them. Local schools may be better or worse than the national picture.

More detail on this slide

These are the latest national figures from the annual State of Computer Science Education report (Code.org with the Computer Science Teachers Association and the ECEP Alliance), published December 2025. About 60 percent of public high schools offered a foundational computer science course, and about 6 percent of high school students were enrolled in one. The share of schools offering it has flattened compared with earlier years. The point is not that schools are failing; it is that most children will meet very little computer science in school, so a gentle start at home can help.

A question parents often ask

Does our local school teach coding?
It varies a lot by school. It is worth asking; our course works alongside school, not instead of it.

Source: Code.org et al. (2025); national data, 2024–25 school year.

With AI, understanding code matters more

In plain language

“Not statistically significant” means the difference was small enough that it could be down to chance. One study of 69 children cannot settle the question.

More detail on this slide

Many parents ask: if AI can write code, why learn? Two pieces of evidence. First, a controlled study at the University of Toronto with 69 learners aged 10 to 17: half had an AI code generator while learning Python. Those with AI completed more tasks and scored higher while learning, and they did not get worse at editing code by hand. A week later, on tests without AI, the difference was small and not statistically significant. Second, the OECD’s 2026 Digital Education Outlook warns that general-purpose chatbots can raise performance on tasks without producing lasting learning, while tools designed for learning (giving hints, asking questions) do better. Our course uses no online AI tools; in Level 3 the children build tiny AI models by hand so they understand how AI learns and where it fails.

A question parents often ask

Should my child use ChatGPT for homework?
Not for this course. The homework is about thinking through the problem; we teach how AI works in Level 3 instead.

Source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023); OECD (2026).

What the research shows

What studies of children learning to code have found. We mark each finding as strong, mixed or an open question, and we say what is not known.

What coding builds, and how sure we are

In plain language

Each badge uses a color, an icon and a word, so it reads the same in black and white. “Strong” means several careful studies and reviews agree. “Mixed” means results vary or shrink with stronger study designs. “Open” means we simply do not know yet.

More detail on this slide

This slide is the honest summary of the whole evidence section. Read the rows from top to bottom: we are most confident about what is closest to coding itself. Children reliably learn to program and to think in steps. There is good evidence for gains in problem solving and planning, especially on tasks that resemble coding. Effects on math, creativity and reasoning are positive on average but shrink in the most careful studies, so we call them mixed. Reading and school grades benefit least. Whether coding builds general persistence or teamwork is an open question: few studies measure it well.

A question parents often ask

So will it help with math?
Possibly a little, and especially with problem solving, but we do not promise better math grades. Think of it as its own valuable subject.

Source: Scherer et al. (2019); Scherer et al. (2020); Montuori et al. (2024); Wing (2006).

The biggest review: 105 studies

In plain language

A meta-analysis pools many studies to find the overall pattern. When effects get smaller in better-designed studies, part of the “benefit” in weaker studies may come from simply doing something new and fun, not from coding itself.

More detail on this slide

This is the largest review of whether learning to program helps other kinds of thinking. Scherer, Siddiq and Sánchez Viveros combined 105 studies with 539 results. Skills closest to programming improved most. Gains also appeared for creative thinking, math and metacognition (thinking about your own thinking), and to a lesser degree spatial skills and reasoning. Reading and school achievement benefited least. Importantly, studies that compared coders with children who did nothing at all found bigger effects than studies with an active comparison group, and published studies showed bigger effects than unpublished ones. That is a reason to be modest. A companion review by the same team (2020, 139 interventions) found a large effect of teaching on programming skill itself.

A question parents often ask

What is “thinking about thinking”?
Metacognition: noticing how you are solving a problem and changing strategy when it isn’t working. Debugging practices exactly this.

Source: Scherer et al. (2019) (105 studies, 539 effects); Scherer et al. (2020).

Where coding seems to help most

In plain language

An effect size compares the average improvement of the coding group with the comparison group, in units of how spread out children’s scores are. 0.89 means a big difference; 0.17 a small one. Because the review pooled only 11 studies, we label it mixed rather than strong.

More detail on this slide

This 2024 review looked only at experiments with children: 19 studies with 1,523 participants, of which 11 could be combined. The pooled effects were large for problem solving (0.89), smaller for planning (0.36), and small for working memory (0.20) and inhibition, the ability to stop an automatic response (0.17). The dashed lines show common rules of thumb: 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.

A question parents often ask

Is 0.89 a lot?
Yes, it is large by usual standards, but it comes from a small number of studies, so treat it as promising rather than proven.

Source: Montuori et al. (2024); pooled (fixed-effect) estimates from 11 studies.

A closer look: one fair test

In plain language

Random assignment is the gold standard: because chance decides who codes, differences at the end are much more likely to be caused by the coding itself. Still, it is one short study of six-year-olds, so we should not assume the same size of effect for our ten-year-olds.

More detail on this slide

This is one of the cleanest studies in the field. Researchers in Italy randomly assigned ten first-grade classes either to eight hours of coding over four weeks (using Code.org puzzles) or to their usual STEM lessons. Before and after, children did planning puzzles such as the Tower of London and tests of inhibition, the ability to stop an automatic response. The coding group improved more, especially in planning; the effect on inhibition was smaller.

A question parents often ask

Why show a study of six-year-olds?
Because it is one of the few truly randomized trials. Studies of older children mostly point the same way but with weaker designs.

Source: Arfé et al. (2020), a cluster-randomized controlled trial.

Early experiences shape interest

In plain language

Correlation versus causation: children who already love science might both expect a science career and later study it. The early expectation might not cause the degree; it might just be an early sign of it. The 2006 study is also old (data from 1988 to 2000).

More detail on this slide

Three findings about interest. First, in a University of Washington experiment, first graders who programmed a small robot showed no gender gap in technology interest and confidence afterwards, while in the comparison groups boys reported more of both. The short activity did not change children’s stereotypes, though. Second, a large US study followed students from eighth grade (1988) into college: those who expected a science-related career at age 13 to 14 were roughly two to three times as likely to graduate with a science degree. This is a correlation (an association), not proof that early interest causes the degree. Third, a 2016 Google–Gallup survey found girls are less likely than boys to be told by parents and teachers that they would be good at computer science.

A question parents often ask

My daughter says coding is for boys. What can I do?
Encourage her as much as you would a son, and point out the variety of people who code. Our course never assigns roles by gender.

Source: Master et al. (2017); Tai et al. (2006); Google & Gallup (2016).

What we don't know (yet)

In plain language

“Transfer” means using a skill learned in one area somewhere else. Near transfer (to similar problems) is common; far transfer (to unrelated subjects) is rare for any activity.

More detail on this slide

This is the most important slide for trust. Researchers have argued about this since the 1980s: Pea and Kurland at Bank Street College questioned the hope that programming automatically improves general thinking, and early studies with the Logo language were disappointing when there was no deliberate teaching. (That critique is old, which we flag, but its lesson still holds.) A 2017 review of chess, music and memory training found the same general pattern: skills rarely carry over to unrelated areas, and apparent effects shrink in better-designed studies. So our promise is modest: children will become capable, confident beginner programmers and practice problem solving. Anything beyond that is a bonus.

A question parents often ask

Then why bother?
Because coding is worth learning for its own sake, like music or a language, and because the way we teach it (projects, teamwork, debugging) builds good learning habits.

Source: Pea & Kurland (1984) (an early critique); Sala & Gobet (2017); Scherer et al. (2019).

What good teaching looks like

Research is clearer about how to teach coding than about its spill-over benefits. These ideas shape how our course is taught.

Six principles the evidence supports

More detail on this slide

Research is clearer about how to teach coding than about its spill-over benefits. These six principles come up again and again. The next three slides give the evidence for each, and then we show where each one appears in our course. The small label in the corner of each card names the key source.

A question parents often ask

Is there one best way to teach coding?
No single method wins everywhere, but these ingredients are consistently linked to better learning and motivation.

Create, don't just consume

In plain language

These are design principles from experienced researchers rather than results of one experiment. They are widely used in computing education because they keep children engaged.

More detail on this slide

Seymour Papert at MIT argued in 1980 that children learn best by building things that matter to them. The Scratch team (Resnick and colleagues, 2009) turned this into three design goals: a low floor (easy to start), a high ceiling (room for complex projects) and wide walls (many kinds of project, so every child finds an interest). Lee and colleagues (2011) describe a progression called Use–Modify–Create: first play with a working program, then change it, then design your own. Our lessons follow exactly that pattern.

A question parents often ask

My child only wants to make games. Is that OK?
Yes. Games are a great vehicle: they need loops, conditions, variables and debugging. Art and data projects are there for others.

Source: Papert (1980); Resnick et al. (2009); Lee et al. (2011).

Learn together, fix bugs on purpose

In plain language

You may hear a famous figure of 0.79 for feedback (Hattie and Timperley, 2007). A later, larger re-analysis by the same research group found about 0.48, which is still a solid effect. We quote the more careful estimate qualitatively.

More detail on this slide

Pair programming means two children share one computer: the driver types, the navigator reads, plans and spots mistakes, and they swap regularly. A 2017 review of 18 studies (mostly university courses) found better results for pairs on assignments, exams and staying in the course, though not on attitudes. A study of 320 middle-school students (Denner and colleagues, 2014) found pairs gained more programming knowledge, especially children with less experience. Debugging: a German classroom study found that explicitly teaching a systematic process for finding bugs improved both debugging performance and students’ confidence compared with practice alone. Feedback: a 2020 review of 435 studies found a solid medium-sized effect on learning, largest when feedback gives information about the task and how to improve, and smaller for praise alone.

A question parents often ask

What if my child does not get along with their partner?
We rotate pairs, set clear roles and swap every few minutes. With an odd number, a trio uses driver, navigator and tester.

Source: Umapathy & Ritzhaupt (2017); Denner et al. (2014); Michaeli & Romeike (2019); Wisniewski et al. (2020).

Off-screen first, read before writing, return often

In plain language

Reading code before writing it is like reading books before writing stories: it builds a picture of how programs work, so writing becomes less frustrating.

More detail on this slide

Unplugged activities teach computing ideas without a computer: acting out a loop as a dance, sorting cards, giving a parent-robot exact instructions. A Spanish study with early primary pupils found that starting with unplugged activities before moving to the computer helped computational thinking and motivation. PRIMM (Predict, Run, Investigate, Modify, Make) asks students to read and predict what code does before writing their own; an evaluation in 13 UK schools with 493 students aged 11 to 14 found better post-test results than a comparison group. The spiral curriculum idea comes from psychologist Jerome Bruner (1960): return to big ideas repeatedly, at greater depth each time.

A question parents often ask

Isn’t time away from the computer wasted?
No. Off-screen activities make the ideas concrete and give eyes a break; they are short and always lead into building.

Source: Olmo-Muñoz et al. (2020); Sentance et al. (2019); Bruner (1960).

Kids Coding

A free course for children from Grade 5: make games and art, first with Scratch blocks, then with Python. One 60-minute session a week.

No accounts, no ads, no tracking.
